queue.sentence: The question
The short answer

On which kinds work best, the material here does not settle the matter, because evidence on changing schools, institutions and policies is thin compared with evidence on building individual learners' skills.
What the evidence covers and what it shows
Why the question matters

In sub-Saharan Africa, pupils with developmental disabilities are described as remaining mostly unschooled, often excluded from mainstream education and facing barriers to enrolment in special schools, which are usually few, expensive, located in the capital and low in capacity [4].

According to the source, the evidence gap map (EGM) summarized there "provides a starting point for researchers, decision makers and programme managers to access the available research evidence on the effectiveness of interventions for people with disabilities in LMICs in order to guide policy and programme activity, and encourage a more strategic, policy-oriented approach to setting the future research agenda" [2].

The source states that the report illustrates the critical value of evaluating and publishing evidence from disability inclusive TPD interventions in LMICs, including any that are ongoing, or are components of highly resource intensive large-scale education sector programs [3].

The source, titled "Teacher professional development for disability inclusion in low‐ and middle‐income Asia‐Pacific countries: An evidence and gap map," presents an evidence and gap map on that topic, and the text provided contains no findings or certainty or confidence wording to quote [3].
The evidence leans towards fixing individuals rather than systems

An evidence and gap map of disability interventions in low- and middle-income countries found that studies focus on fixing individuals, for instance by improving social or learning skills, and that fewer studies focus on improving infrastructure or institutions [2].
That map describes the absence of evidence on what works to promote disability inclusion as a very striking gap [2].

A separate evidence map on teacher training likewise notes that most research in this space focuses on interventions that try to improve skills in students with disabilities rather than addressing institutional or environmental barriers [3].
Gaps in where and for whom the evidence exists
The evidence and gap map reports that most studies come from upper-middle-income countries and that there is limited evidence from low-income countries [2].
It also says more studies are needed on all types of impairment, including visual and hearing impairments [2].
Teacher training

An evidence and gap map found 50 studies on teacher training for the inclusion of students with disabilities in low- and middle-income Asia-Pacific countries, with only 16 of 41 countries reporting evidence on in-service teacher professional development for disability inclusion [3].
That map found no studies reporting on how teachers could support positive student behaviour [3].

One included example was a one-day teacher workshop in an inclusive education programme, which is reported to have influenced students' perspectives of themselves and developed their social awareness skills [3].
What teachers and families in sub-Saharan Africa report

A systematic review of 32 qualitative articles from seven sub-Saharan African countries found that unclear policies and insufficient training, resources and support for teachers often blocked the implementation of inclusive education [4].

The review's authors note that most studies were conducted in the southern region of sub-Saharan Africa, with South Africa accounting for half of the research included, "possibly limiting the transferability of results to other countries and communities" [4].

Inadequate teacher skills and confidence for inclusive education were reported in 15 studies, but there was a similar number of indications that teachers' skills, confidence and attitudes towards inclusion could improve through training and, more frequently, experience [4].

The review found in-service training on inclusive education equally lacking in all countries studied and, when available, it often failed to provide specific skills and knowledge on developmental disabilities [4].
Factors in favour of inclusive education included the commitment of many teachers and the work of non-governmental organisations, which provided resources and training [4].
A related review reported large class sizes of 40 to 80 students under a single teacher as a striking everyday challenge for including children with developmental disabilities [5].

The review's authors suggest that a broader focus on whole-class approaches compared to individualized attention, in line with indigenous perspectives, may reduce the impact of challenges posed by large class sizes [5].
That review found that teachers' inclusion efforts appeared progressive but were mostly based on Western pedagogies and were challenged by limited resources and training [5].

The authors of that review caution that the transferability of their synthesis is limited because the studies it drew on showed a high prevalence of research from South Africa, which is substantially better-resourced than most other sub-Saharan African countries and arguably the one most prominently influenced by Western cultures [5].

The review reports that studies "aimed at improving the accessibility of learning environments in education reported positive impacts of these interventions on teacher knowledge and attitudes, parent knowledge and attitudes, and violence reduction" [1].
What holds up

The best-supported claim is the 2025 systematic review's conclusion that a range of individual-level interventions work to improve educational outcomes for people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries [1].
An evidence and gap map and other reviews agree that research concentrates on building individual skills, leaving school-level, systemic and institutional approaches under-studied [1, 2, 3].
The sub-Saharan African review suggests that motivated teachers should be given appropriate training, resources and support, directly and by promoting the work of non-governmental organisations [4].
The other African review proposes that training based on indigenous pedagogies could improve the use and outcomes of inclusive strategies [5].
Both of these recommendations rest on reviews of qualitative studies of stakeholder views and experiences rather than on tested effects [4, 5].

The sub-Saharan African review also notes a gap in its evidence base, concluding that future research should explore attitudes towards mainstream education of the majority of children with developmental disabilities in sub-Saharan Africa, who cannot access school or drop out, and their parents [4].
Because evidence from low-income countries and on many impairment types is limited, claims about which kinds of programme work best should be treated as unsettled [2].
